Built-up land, artificial surfaces 2. Cropland 3. Grassland 4. Tree-covered areas 5. Shrub-covered areas 6. Shrub/Herbaceous, regularly flooded 7. Tree-covered, regularly flooded, saline 8. layers.title: Share of land by slope class
layers.description: The terrain slope information has been compiled using elevation data from ALOS World 3D - 30m (AW3D30) provided by [Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, JAXA](https://www.eorc.jaxa.jp/ALOS/en/dataset/aw3d30/aw3d30_e.htm). Terrain slopes (%) are calculated at 30 arc-seconds and grouped into ten slope gradient classes: 0–0.5%, 0.5–2%, 2–5%, 5–8%, 8–12%, 12–16%, 16–24%, 24–30%, 30–45%, and >45%. Each raster represents the share of land area within a 30 arc-second grid cell belonging to the corresponding slope class. Raster values range from 0 to 10,000, representing land-area shares of 0% to 100%, scaled by a factor of 100. Divide the raster values by 100 to obtain percentages.

layers.title: Most limiting soil quality
layers.description: Results on most limiting soil quality (SQ) for agricultural production are mapped at an approximate spatial resolution of 1 km. Each grid cell is classified according to the soil or terrain factor that imposes the strongest constraint on land suitability. The assessment is based on soil and terrain attributes from the Harmonized World Soils Database version 2.01 (HWSD v2.01; FAO & IIASA. 2023) and processed through the Global Agro-Ecological Zoning (GAEZ) framework. Soil suitability is determined through crop-specific evaluations of seven major soil qualities relevant to agriculture: - SQ1: Nutrient availability - SQ2: Nutrient retention capacity - SQ3: Rooting conditions - SQ4: Oxygen availability for roots - SQ5: Presence of salinity and sodicity - SQ6: Presence of lime and gypsum - SQ7: Workability Soil qualities have been estimated for the dominant soils in each grid cell, using maize as the reference crop. Each soil quality is evaluated by comparing soil attributes against crop-specific requirements under different input and management levels. The GAEZ methodology integrates these evaluations and identifies the most limiting soil quality for each grid cell, the resulting map is a categorical classification, where each pixel represents the soil quality (or terrain constraint) that most strongly limits agricultural suitability at that location. This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Land and Water Resources theme and Soil Resources sub-theme. For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

layers.title: Soil suitability rating
layers.description: The Soil Suitability Rating (SSR) dataset provides a spatial assessment of soil suitability and associated constraints for agricultural production under conventional farming systems at an approximate spatial resolution of 1 km. Developed within the Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 5 (GAEZ v5) framework, the dataset quantifies soil-related limitations to crop production based on crop-specific soil requirements and different levels of agricultural inputs and management. The assessment uses soil attributes derived from the Harmonized World Soil Database version 22 (HWSD v2.2; FAO & IIASA, 2026) and evaluates seven major soil qualities: nutrient availability (SQ1), nutrient retention capacity (SQ2), rooting conditions (SQ3), oxygen availability to roots (SQ4), salinity and sodicity (SQ5), calcium carbonate and gypsum content (SQ6), and soil workability (SQ7). Nutrient availability is given greater importance under low-input conditions, nutrient retention capacity under high-input conditions, and both are weighted equally under intermediate-input conditions. The remaining five soil qualities are combined using a multiplicative function that emphasizes the most limiting soil quality while accounting for the average of the remaining soil qualities. Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020. For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100. The ratio (%) compares the amount of incoming precipitation to the evaporative demand of the reference crop assumed in the calculation of the Penman-Monteith equation used for reference evapotranspiration ETo. An index value of 100% means that precipitation equals reference potential evapotranspiration, i.e. that precipitation on average over the year matches the evaporative demand of the vegetation. Values below 100% indicate the occurrence of some water deficit; values above 100% mean that precipitation exceeds evaporative demand on an annual basis. The annual P/PET dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Moisture Regime sub-theme. layers.title: Koeppen-Geiger (2-character) classification
layers.description: The Koeppen-Geiger climate classification is based on a subdivision of terrestrial climates into five major types, which are represented by the capital letters A (tropical), B (dry), C (temperate), D (cold), and E (polar). Each of these climate types, except for B, is defined by temperature criteria. Type B designates climates in which the controlling factor on vegetation is dryness (rather than coldness). Dry climates are divided into arid (BW) and semi-arid (BS) subtypes. Other climate types are sub-divided according to seasonal precipitation characteristics. The level-2 classification distinguishes 14 classes. The Koeppen-Geiger climate classification dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods. Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020. For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100. The air frost number dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Climate Classification sub-theme. layers.title: Permafrost zones
layers.description: In GAEZ, the procedures proposed by Nelson and Outcalt (1987) are applied to calculate an air frost index (FI) which is used to characterize climate-derived permafrost conditions into four classes: (i) Continuous permafrost (ii) Discontinuous permafrost (iii) Sporadic permafrost (iv) No permafrost Reference permafrost zones are determined based on prevailing daily mean air temperature (Ta). The air frost index (FI) is calculated and used to characterize permafrost areas. For this calculation, accumulated degree-days, above and below 0 °C, are used to calculate the thawing index (DDT) and the freezing index (DDF). layers.description: Results on harvested area for the year 2020, are provided in hectares at a global scale with approximately 10 km spatial resolution for 38 major crops/crop groups [(see Appendix 4-1 of the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation)](https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki/14.-Appendix-4%E2%80%901-Crops), separately in rain-fed, irrigated or total cropland. Apparent yield gaps are closely related to the calculated yield achievement factors, together summing up to 100 percent.
